title: Schedulability Analysis and Priority Assignment for Segmented Self-Suspending Tasks

extraction.paper_name: Schedulability Analysis and Priority Assignment for Segmented Self-Suspending Tasks
extraction.paper_description: The paper introduces a pseudo-polynomial time schedulability test (SCAIR) for segmented self-suspending tasks under fixed-priority scheduling. It defines a multi-segment workload function to bound interference and proves the test is compatible with Audsley's Optimal Priority Assignment (OPA).

formal_description.statement: W_i_h_t = sum_{q=h-1}^{lambda-1} C_i_((q mod M_i) + 1) + min(C_i_((lambda mod M_i) + 1), t - sum_{q=h-1}^{lambda-1} (C_i_((q mod M_i) + 1) + S_i_q)) where lambda is the maximum integer satisfying sum_{q=h-1}^{lambda-1} (C_i_((q mod M_i) + 1) + S_i_q) <= t. S_i_q is the separation time: S_i_((q mod M_i) + 1) if within the same job, T_i - D_i if it is the last segment of a carry-in job, and T_i - (C_i + S_i) otherwise.

variables.W_i_h_t: Multi-segment workload function for task tau_i starting at segment h over interval t
variables.C_i_j: Worst-case execution time of the j-th computation segment of task tau_i
variables.S_i_j: Maximum suspension time of the j-th suspension interval of task tau_i
variables.M_i: Number of computation segments in task tau_i
variables.T_i: Minimum inter-arrival time (period) of task tau_i

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the workload contributed by a higher-priority task tau_i starting from a specific segment h.

informal_sketch.intuition: Calculates how much execution time a higher-priority task can force onto a lower-priority one, starting the count from any arbitrary segment of the first (carry-in) job.
steps: Identify the starting segment index h
Iteratively add computation segments and the required separation (suspension or inter-job gap)
Stop when the total time elapsed exceeds the interval t
Add the partial execution of the final segment that overlaps with the end of the interval
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def compute_multi_segment_workload(tau_i, h, t):
    workload = 0
    elapsed_time = 0
    current_q = h - 1
    while True:
        seg_idx = (current_q % tau_i.M_i) + 1
        c_val = tau_i.C[seg_idx]
        
        if seg_idx < tau_i.M_i:
            s_sep = tau_i.S[seg_idx]
        elif current_q < tau_i.M_i:
            s_sep = tau_i.T - tau_i.D
        else:
            s_sep = tau_i.T - (tau_i.C_total + tau_i.S_total)
            
        if elapsed_time + c_val + s_sep > t:
            remaining = t - elapsed_time
            workload += min(c_val, max(0, remaining))
            break
        
        workload += c_val
        elapsed_time += c_val + s_sep
        current_q += 1
    return workload
key_insights: The separation time S_i_q changes depending on whether the next segment belongs to the same job or a subsequent job release.

variables.W_i_t: Maximum workload function for task tau_i over interval t

formal_description.conclusion: Defines the upper bound of interference from task tau_i regardless of which segment aligns with the start of the interval.

informal_sketch.intuition: Since we don't know which segment of a higher-priority task will first interfere with our task, we check all possible starting segments and take the worst case.
steps: For each segment j from 1 to M_i
Calculate the workload assuming segment j is the first to appear in the interval
The maximum of these values is the safe upper bound
key_insights: This eliminates the need to find a specific 'critical instant' which is non-trivial for self-suspending tasks.

formal_description.statement: A_i_t <= W_i_h_t for all t >= 0, given a carry-in job released no later than t_0 and its h-th segment released no earlier than t_0.

variables.A_i_t: Accumulated execution time of tau_i in interval [t_0, t_0 + t]

formal_description.conclusion: W_i_h_t is a safe upper bound for the case where the h-th segment starts at or after the interval beginning.

informal_sketch.intuition: If a segment starts exactly at or after the start of our observation window, the workload function correctly counts all subsequent execution segments and their required gaps.
steps: Compare the actual schedule execution A_i_t with the constructed worst-case W_i_h_t
Show that shifting segments earlier in the workload function only increases the total work in the window
key_insights: The assumption R_i <= T_i ensures that jobs of the same task do not overlap in execution.

formal_description.statement: A_i_t <= W_i_h_t for all t >= 0, given a carry-in job released no later than t_0 and its h-th segment released before t_0 but not finished at t_0.

variables.A_i_t: Accumulated execution time of tau_i in interval [t_0, t_0 + t]

formal_description.conclusion: W_i_h_t remains a safe upper bound even if a segment is already partially executed when the interval starts.

informal_sketch.intuition: If a segment is already running when we start looking, the 'worst case' is that it just started, which is already covered by the workload function starting at that segment.
steps: Assume segment h has been running for time y before t_0
Show that the work in [t_0, t_0 + t] is less than the work in [t_0 - y, t_0 - y + t] where the segment starts exactly at the beginning
key_insights: Starting a segment exactly at t_0 always provides more workload than having it partially finished.

formal_description.statement: For any interval length t, there exists a computation segment C_i_h with h in {1, ..., M_i} such that the work of tau_i in [t_0, t_0 + t) is bounded by W_i_h_t.
formal_description.conclusion: The multi-segment workload function is a sufficient bound for interference.

informal_sketch.intuition: Combines Lemma 1 and Lemma 2 to cover all possible states a task can be in at the start of an interference interval.
steps: At any time t_0, a task is either not executing, or some segment h is executing/ready
If not executing, the next segment to release is some h (Lemma 1)
If executing, some segment h is currently active (Lemma 2)
key_insights: This theorem justifies using the maximum over all h as a safe total interference bound.

formal_description.statement: R_star_k = C_k + S_hat_k + sum_{tau_i in hp_tau_k} W_i_R_star_k

variables.R_star_k: Worst-case response time of task tau_k
variables.S_hat_k: Total maximum suspension time of tau_k
variables.hp_tau_k: Set of tasks with higher priority than tau_k
variables.W_i_R_star_k: Maximum workload function of tau_i over interval R_star_k

formal_description.conclusion: Provides a response time bound using the 'Suspension as Computation' (SC) approach.

informal_sketch.intuition: Treats the task's own suspension time as if it were actual execution time. This simplifies the task into a non-suspending one for analysis purposes.
steps: Combine all computation segments and suspension intervals into one large execution block
Use fixed-point iteration to find the response time, adding interference from higher-priority tasks using the max workload function
key_insights: Simple but can be very pessimistic if suspension times are long.

formal_description.statement: R_k_j = C_k_j + sum_{tau_i in hp_tau_k} W_i_R_k_j

variables.R_k_j: Response time of the j-th computation segment of task tau_k
variables.C_k_j: Execution time of the j-th segment of tau_k
variables.W_i_R_k_j: Maximum workload function of tau_i over interval R_k_j

formal_description.conclusion: Calculates the response time for a single computation segment of a self-suspending task.

informal_sketch.intuition: Instead of looking at the whole task, we look at just one piece of execution. This piece only suffers interference while it is ready to run.
steps: Start with the segment's own execution time
Iteratively add interference from higher-priority tasks until the value converges
key_insights: This assumes that every time a segment finishes and the task suspends, the interference 'restarts' for the next segment.

variables.R_star_k: Worst-case response time of task tau_k
variables.S_hat_k: Total maximum suspension time of tau_k
variables.R_k_j: Response time of segment j from Lemma 3

formal_description.conclusion: Provides a response time bound using the 'As Interference Restarts' (AIR) approach.

informal_sketch.intuition: The total time from task release to completion is the sum of the time spent in each computation segment (including interference) plus the time spent suspending.
steps: Calculate the response time for every individual computation segment using Lemma 3
Sum these response times together
Add the total maximum suspension time of the task
key_insights: This is often tighter than SC when suspension intervals are long relative to higher-priority task periods.

formal_description.statement: tau_k is schedulable if min(R_star_k_SC, R_star_k_AIR) <= D_k

informal_sketch.intuition: Since both SC and AIR provide safe upper bounds, we can take the minimum of the two. If either one is within the deadline, the task is guaranteed to be schedulable.
steps: Compute response time using the SC method
Compute response time using the AIR method
Check if the smaller of the two is less than or equal to the deadline
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def is_SCAIR_schedulable(tau_k, hp_tasks):
    r_sc = calculate_R_SC(tau_k, hp_tasks)
    r_air = calculate_R_AIR(tau_k, hp_tasks)
    return min(r_sc, r_air) <= tau_k.D
key_insights: Combining the two methods covers a wider range of task parameters effectively.

formal_description.statement: A test is OPA-compatible if: 1) It depends on the set of hp_tasks but not their order. 2) It depends on the set of lp_tasks but not their order. 3) Swapping a task to a higher priority cannot make it unschedulable if it was previously schedulable.
formal_description.conclusion: Criteria for using Audsley's Optimal Priority Assignment algorithm.

informal_sketch.intuition: A schedulability test is OPA-compatible if the priority of a task only matters relative to whether other tasks are 'above' or 'below' it, and having fewer/weaker competitors always helps.
steps: Check if the test formula treats all higher-priority tasks as a set
Check if lower-priority tasks are ignored
Check for monotonicity with respect to priority
key_insights: OPA-compatibility allows finding the optimal priority assignment in O(n^2) instead of O(n!).

formal_description.conclusion: SCAIR can be used with Audsley's algorithm.

informal_sketch.intuition: The workload functions and response time calculations in SCAIR only sum up the interference from the set of higher-priority tasks; the internal order of those tasks doesn't change the sum.
steps: Observe that sum_{tau_i in hp_tau_k} W_i_t is independent of the order of i
Observe that lower priority tasks do not appear in the equations
Observe that moving a task from hp_tau_k to lp_tau_k reduces the interference sum
key_insights: This is the key to making the analysis practical for large task sets.

formal_description.statement: If any priority assignment exists for which Theorem 4 holds, SCAIR-OPA returns one of them.
formal_description.conclusion: SCAIR-OPA is an optimal priority assignment for the SCAIR test.

informal_sketch.intuition: Because the test is OPA-compatible, Audsley's algorithm is guaranteed to find a valid priority ordering if one exists.
steps: Apply Audsley's OPA algorithm using Theorem 4 as the 'is_schedulable' check
key_insights: Optimality here is relative to the specific schedulability test, not necessarily the physical system.
